rules.check: Every symbol the trade's plans show in the area exists in the model; nothing is missing.
how: Look at each trade plan crop of the area (and the enlarged plan when there is one) and list every symbol inside the area with its tag.
Find each listed symbol in the model picture and the object list (same kind, near the same place).
A symbol with no model element is a 'missing' finding; cite the print crop and where on it the symbol is.
The prescreen has already matched the symbols the job read (objects.json `prescreen`, G-PRESENT): start from its missing and extra findings and check the symbols the job did not read.

examples.pass: The power plan shows four receptacles in the room; the model has four receptacles there.
examples.fail: The power plan shows a receptacle by the desk; the model has nothing within reach of that spot.

rules.check: Every model element in the area traces to a print symbol or note; nothing is extra.
how: Go through the object list for the area; each element names its source sheet and point.
Look at that place on the cited print crop: the symbol or note must be there.
An element with no source, or whose source shows nothing, is an 'extra' finding.

examples.pass: A duplex receptacle's source is the power plan at the wall by the bed, and the symbol is there.
examples.fail: A second light fixture sits in the corridor stretch; no RCP or note shows a fixture there.

rules.check: Each element is within tolerance of its print location once the sheet is laid on the plan.
how: Compare the model-over-print overlay crop: each model element should sit on its symbol.
Measure from walls or grid lines both on the print and in the model when the offset is not obvious.
An element farther than the tolerance from its symbol is a 'fail' with the distance and direction.

examples.pass: The switch sits 3 in from where the symbol is drawn.
examples.fail: The panel is drawn on the corridor wall but the model has it 4 ft along on the next wall.

rules.check: Each plan keynote marker in the area whose note calls for an object (a box of a size, a device, conduit of a size, a sleeve) has that object in the model at the marker, and conduit a keynote calls for has the size and route the note gives (pull tape, above a hard-lid ceiling, in the corridor, a riser between the floors).
how: objects.json `keynotes` holds the keynote lists of the sheets that mark this area (number and note) and each marker in or by it; the prescreen (G-KEYNOTE) has matched each note's call to the model within route_ft of its marker. Start from its findings.
Look at each marker's crop (its number in a hexagon or circle, and what its leader points at) and read the note in the keynote list crop.
A box, device or sleeve the note calls for with nothing of that kind and size at the marker is 'missing', citing the note's number and text and the marker; a box of another size is a 'fail'.
Keynote conduit: the size, pull tape and route the note gives; a riser goes up to the next floor's box. Each rated wall or floor it passes is listed with the rating its firestopping must keep.

examples.pass: Keynote 2 calls for an 8"x8"x6" junction box and 1" conduit with pull tape above the corridor's ceiling; the model has the box 2 ft from the marker and 1" conduit above the 9 ft ceiling in the corridor.
examples.fail: Keynote 5 calls for a 12"x12"x6" pull box; the box at its marker is 4"x4"x2-1/8".

rules.check: Every below-grade or under-slab callout of the documents (a note, a keynote, a site plan's callout) has its run in the model and on an underground sheet, of the size, count, material and least depth it gives; every stub-up has two dimensions to a slab corner or edge or a grid line; a run CADaddy proposes is reported as proposed with its review item, never as called; a buried run no callout, drawing or proposal accounts for is extra.
how: objects.json `underground` lists the callouts read off the sheets (what each calls for: trade, count, size, material, least depth, what it serves), the underground sheets (the set's own, and the ones CADaddy generated: `underground_sheet` prints) and the buried runs and stub-ups; the prescreen (G-UNDERGROUND) matched each callout to a run. Start from its findings.

Read each callout on its sheet's crop and the run that answers it on the underground sheet's run schedule: the count, the trade size, the material (PVC Schedule 40 or 80, rigid steel) and the depth to the top of the run; a run shallower than the callout's least depth, or of another size or material, is a 'fail' citing the note.

A callout with no run in the model, or a run no underground sheet shows, is 'missing'. A dashed run marked PROPOSED is CADaddy's, not the documents': it never answers a callout; report it 'unsure' citing its RFI.
On the stub-up schedule and the plan, each stub-up has two perpendicular dimensions from a slab edge or corner or a grid line; one or none is a 'fail'.

examples.pass: The site plan's note calls for two 5" Schedule 40 PVC conduits at least 48" below grade; the model has both at 48" and the underground sheet's run schedule lists them.
examples.fail: The note calls for 48" below grade; the run is 24" deep. The stub-up at the floor box has a dimension from the slab's west edge only.

rules.check: Every kind of object the documents define (a legend or schedule row, an abbreviation, a keynote or note naming an object) and the plans mark is in the model, about as many as the plans show; a kind the electrical, fire alarm or low-voltage sheets connect to (power, a circuit, a module, a data drop) is in the model even when its own trade is by others.
how: objects.json `prescreen` G-COVERAGE findings list each kind the documents define with its plan marks by sheet and level and the model's count of it; a kind with marks and no element is ranked first. Start from them.

On this area's print crops, look for tags or symbols of a kind the model's picture and object list hold none of (a damper tag on a duct, a device symbol the legend names): that is a 'missing' finding naming the kind, citing the print crop (prints/…) and the legend or abbreviation that defines it.

A kind the electrical or fire alarm sheets power, circuit or give a module to must be in the model whatever trade furnishes it: report it 'missing' citing the electrical sheet's note and the plan that tags it.
Every answer cites a print page (a prints/ picture with its sheet); a finding that cites none is kept as 'unsure'.

examples.pass: The mechanical legend defines FSD as a combination fire/smoke damper; the mechanical plans tag five of them, and the model holds five fire/smoke dampers.
examples.fail: The plans tag five FSD, the electrical keynote powers them, and the model has no damper at all.

rules.check: The element's type mark matches the symbol's tag and the legend or schedule row it points to.
how: Read the tag beside the symbol on the plan crop.
Find that tag's row in the legend or schedule crop and note its description.
The element's type mark and properties in the object list must be that row; a different mark or description is a 'fail'.

examples.pass: The fixture tagged A on the RCP is type A in the model, and schedule row A is a 2x4 troffer.
examples.fail: The fixture tagged B on the RCP is type A in the model.

rules.check: The element is in the room it serves on the print.
how: Note the room the symbol is drawn in on the plan crop (the room tag and its walls).
The object list gives the element's room; they must be the same room.
An element on the wrong side of a wall is a 'fail' even when it is within the placement tolerance.

examples.pass: A bath exhaust fan drawn in the bathroom is in the bathroom in the model.
examples.fail: A receptacle drawn on the bedroom side of a wall is placed on the corridor side.

rules.check: A wall-hosted item is in the wall the print shows, on the face toward the room it serves; a ceiling-hosted one (a detector, a ceiling sensor) is in the ceiling of that room.
how: On the plan crop, see which wall line the symbol touches and which side of it the symbol is drawn; a symbol away from the walls (on the RCP or fire alarm plan) is ceiling-hosted.
The object list gives the host wall and face (and the prescreen's G-HOST distance to the face); in the model picture a wall item must be on that wall, facing that room, a ceiling item at the ceiling.
A floating item, the wrong wall, the wrong face, or a ceiling item placed on a wall (or the reverse) is a 'fail'.

examples.pass: A switch drawn inside the room by the door is in that wall, on the room face.
examples.fail: The switch is in the wall but on the corridor face.

rules.check: A wall-mounted item is at the height above its floor that the documents give it (an AFF note, the interior elevation, the legend, the schedule or the general notes).
how: The object list gives each element's height above the floor and the prescreen's G-HEIGHT reading: the height the documents give it and where (height_expected: the sheet, the point and the words; an AFF note by it, the interior elevation, the legend, a schedule, the general notes, or the project rule validate.height.<mark|kind>), and whether its model height is a default no document gives.
Look for an AFF note beside or leadered to the symbol on the enlarged plan, then the interior elevation of that wall, then the legend, schedule or general notes.
A height off by more than the tolerance is a 'fail' citing the note or view; say 'unsure' when no document gives a height.

examples.pass: The elevation notes the desk receptacle at 18 in AFF; the model has it at 18 in.
examples.fail: The enlarged plan notes the counter receptacle at 44 in AFF; the model has it at 18 in.

rules.check: A wall device is placed the way a crew lays it out: on its named wall face (room/side), at the documented height to the stated point of its plate (hard), at its along-face offset from its reference face or object (soft, within its band, solved to a stud side clear of pipes), inside the cabinet or behind the appliance its constraint names, and with its full faceplate clear of casings and other plates.
how: The object list gives each wall device's host_face, height_aff to height_ref, offset_along from offset_from, offset_depth, faceplate, along_band, layout_solve and constraints; the prescreen's G-LAYOUT readings say which part failed (check: face, height, along, constraint, plate).

Compare with the enlarged plan's dimension strings and the interior elevations: the height to the stated point, the distance from the named face or opening edge, the cabinet or appliance it sits in or behind.

A height off by more than the tolerance, an offset outside its band, a plate edge outside its cabinet or appliance footprint, or a plate over a casing or another plate is a 'fail'; 'pending framing' is 'unsure' until the studs and pipes exist.

examples.pass: The microwave receptacle is centred in the upper cabinet within its 2 in band at 66 in AFF, its plate inside the cabinet.
examples.fail: The refrigerator receptacle's plate is 3.5 in past the refrigerator's back footprint: it would show beside the refrigerator.

rules.check: Receptacles are along the wall and at the height where the enlarged plan, interior elevations, furniture plan, legend or general notes put them.
how: Find what each receptacle serves on the enlarged or furniture plan (headboard, desk, counter, TV) and check it is on that wall beside that item.
Read the height from the interior elevation where one shows it, else the legend or general notes, else the standard height note.
Compare the model's height above floor in the object list; outside the tolerance is a 'fail' with both heights.

examples.pass: The elevation shows the counter receptacle 4 in above the backsplash; the model has it at that height over the counter.
examples.fail: The elevation shows the TV receptacle high on the wall; the model has it at the standard low height.

rules.check: Each receptacle is the type the legend, notes and code call for: GFCI near sinks and in wet locations, weather-resistant with a cover outdoors, and USB, quad or floor box as tagged (tamper-resistance is E-RECEPT-TR's).
how: Read the symbol and its subscript tag (GFI, WP, USB, quad) on the plan crop and the matching legend row.
Check the general notes for blanket requirements (GFCI within a distance of a sink, weather-resistant outdoors).
The element's type and properties in the object list must carry every required rating; a missing rating is a 'fail'.

examples.pass: The receptacle beside the vanity is tagged GFI on the plan and is a GFCI type in the model.
examples.fail: The exterior receptacle is a plain duplex in the model; the plan tags it WP.

rules.check: Every 15 or 20 A, 125 V receptacle (duplex, GFCI, USB, quad) in a dwelling unit, guest room, guest suite or other area the code lists is tamper-resistant.
how: The prescreen gives each receptacle's tamper-resistance fact and where it came from: its product record, its legend row or type tag (TR), or a general note or spec line making every receptacle tamper-resistant.
Where it says 'unsure', look for the fact yourself: the TR subscript beside the symbol, the legend row of its tag, the general notes and the wiring device spec section.
A receptacle in such a room that is not tamper-resistant is a 'fail' citing what says so; a GFCI receptacle is checked here as well as by E-RECEPT-TYPE.

examples.pass: The general notes say all receptacles shall be tamper-resistant; the guest room's duplex receptacles pass, citing the note.
examples.fail: The guest room's GFCI receptacle by the vanity is a product the record says is not tamper-resistant.

code.says: In the areas listed, nonlocking 15- and 20-ampere, 125-volt receptacles shall be listed tamper-resistant receptacles.

rules.check: Each product's record matches the documents field by field: its maker is in the approved list (its type's submittal first, else the specification's makers), its catalog number is the one submitted for its type, and its colour or finish, configuration, rating and required features are what its specification section requires.
how: The prescreen gives each element's product fields as the model has them (its properties, its product record, its type) next to what the submittal and the specification require, with the section, page and submittal cited: pass, fail, or unsure ('no product data' when the model doesn't know the field).

Where it says 'unsure', read the specification and submittal pages in the packet: the wiring device, lighting or plumbing fixture section's product paragraph and the submitted cut sheet for the element's type.

A maker not in the approved list, a catalog number other than the submitted one, a colour, configuration or rating other than the specification's, or a missing required feature is a 'fail' citing the page; never pass a field the model doesn't record.

examples.pass: The duplex receptacle's maker and catalog number are the submitted ones, and it is white, 20 A 125 V and tamper-resistant as the wiring device section requires.
examples.fail: The specification says wiring devices are white; the model's receptacle is red.

rules.check: Each receptacle has the features the code requires where it is, from the code rules data the build applies too: tamper-resistant in guest rooms and dwelling units, GFCI protection judged on its whole circuit (a GFCI breaker means a standard device; near a sink or in a listed place on a standard breaker, a GFCI device or one on the load side of a GFCI device of the same circuit), weather-resistant outdoors.
how: The prescreen reads each receptacle's room, its circuit and that breaker's type from the panel schedule, the sinks near it and the places the code lists, and says pass, fail or unsure with the code text and the schedule row cited.
Where it says 'unsure' ('breaker type unknown' or 'no product data'), read the panel schedule row of its circuit and the device's legend row or tag on the plan.
A GFCI receptacle on a GFCI breaker is a 'fail' (double protection); a standard receptacle where GFCI is needed with no GFCI breaker and no GFCI receptacle upstream on its circuit is a 'fail'.

examples.pass: The bath receptacle is a standard device on a GFCI breaker, as the panel schedule row shows.
examples.fail: The kitchenette receptacle beside the sink is a standard device on a standard breaker with no GFCI receptacle ahead of it on the circuit.

rules.check: Switches are on the latch side of the door as drawn, at the legend height.
how: On the plan crop, find the door the switch is by and which side its latch is (opposite the hinge, by the swing arc).
The model switch must be on that side of the opening, within the placement tolerance of the symbol.
Compare the height with the legend or general notes.

examples.pass: The switch is on the latch side of the entry door at the legend height.
examples.fail: The switch is on the hinge side, behind the open door.

rules.check: Panelboards, load centers, transformers and disconnects are where the electrical plan shows them.
how: Find the panel symbol and its tag on the power plan or enlarged electrical room plan.
The model panel with that tag must be on the same wall, within tolerance of the symbol.
The tag must match the panel schedule's name.

examples.pass: The panel tagged on the plan is on the closet's back wall in the model.
examples.fail: The panel is on the side wall of the closet; the plan draws it on the back wall.

rules.check: Panels are recessed or surface mounted as the submittal or panel schedule says; a recessed cabinet fits the depth of its host wall type; the working space in front is kept clear.
how: Read the mounting from the panel schedule header or the submittal page (recessed or surface, cabinet depth).
For a recessed panel, find the host wall's type in the partition legend; its stud depth must hold the cabinet depth.
Check the model: mounting matches, and nothing (wall, equipment, door swing) sits in the clear working space in front of it.

examples.pass: The schedule says recessed, the model panel is recessed in a wall whose studs are deeper than the cabinet, and the space in front is clear.
examples.fail: The submittal shows a surface cabinet but the model recesses it in a wall too thin to hold it.

rules.check: In front of every piece of electrical gear the working space NEC 110.26 calls for is clear of walls, other equipment and door swings (as deep as its voltage to ground and condition call for, as wide as the gear or 30 in, 6.5 ft or the gear's height high), with that headroom to the ceiling, and its dedicated space (its footprint up to 6 ft over it) free of ducts and pipes.
how: objects.json `gear` lists each piece of gear here with its box, its working space as the build laid it out (`properties` WORKING SPACE, PLACEMENT; `sources.status` proposed when CADaddy placed it because the plans don't locate it) and the prescreen's measured clear depth, front face, doors and ceiling (E-GEAR-SPACE in `prescreen`). Start from those findings.

On the enlarged electrical room plan, measure from the gear's front to the nearest wall, equipment or door leaf across the space's width; the depth is 3 ft up to 150 V to ground, and 3, 3.5 or 4 ft from 151 to 600 V for conditions 1, 2 and 3 (what faces the gear: nothing live or grounded, a grounded wall, live parts). A depth that holds only for condition 1 is 'unsure' unless the plan shows what faces the gear.
A door whose leaf sweeps the space when it swings into the room is a 'fail'; one whose swing the plan doesn't show is 'unsure'.
Over the gear's footprint up to 6 ft above it, no duct or pipe of another system may pass (dedicated space); the ceiling must be at least 6.5 ft or the gear's top.

examples.pass: The 208Y/120 V panel has 6 ft clear in front of it, 30 in wide, under a 9 ft ceiling; no duct passes over it.
examples.fail: The room's door swings in across the panel's working space; a sanitary line crosses 4 ft over the switchboard.

rules.check: Each enclosure takes what lands on it, recomputed from the feeder schedule, the one-line and the gear submittal: the raceways through each side fit that side's conduit (knockout) area; the conductors in the wiring gutter fill at most 40 percent of it (NEC 312.8); each lug has the bending space NEC 312.6 gives for its conductors; each feeder's parallel sets, size and metal fit the lugs it lands on.
how: objects.json `gear` gives each piece of gear's feeders (sets, conductors, conduits and trade sizes, entry side, the schedule row and one-line tag each came from), its lugs and the submittal's box and conduit areas. E-GEAR-FILL in `prescreen` packed the raceways on each side and counted the gutter, bending space and lugs; start from those findings.

Check the counts on the feeder schedule and the one-line pictures: every feeder the panel schedule names (a row feeding another panel) must have its conduits and conductors; a missing one makes the count 'unsure'.

Check the conduit area and lugs on the gear submittal pages: a side whose raceways need more area than it has is a 'fail'; a parallel set with more sets than the lugs take, or a size outside the lugs' range, is a 'fail'.
The gutter's width and depth and the bending space at the lugs are rarely in a panelboard submittal: when the submittal doesn't give them they are missing and the finding is 'unsure', never a pass.

examples.pass: Four 2 in conduits come in through the top of a 20 in wide panel whose submittal draws a 16 x 4 in conduit area; its main lugs take two 3/0-500 kcmil per phase and the feeder is two sets of 350 kcmil.
examples.fail: Fourteen raceways come in through the top: about 150 sq in needed, 60 sq in of conduit area. The feeder is four sets of 500 kcmil on lugs that take two per phase.

rules.check: Each piece of gear's enclosure in the model (height, width, depth) is the gear submittal's.
how: objects.json `gear` gives each piece's box as built (`model_in`) and as the submittal gives it (`submittal`, re-read from the job's gear submittals; `properties.BOX` as the build recorded it). E-GEAR-SIZE in `prescreen` compared them.
Read the box on the gear submittal pages (the dimension line or the elevation drawing): a side off by more than the tolerance is a 'fail'; no size in any submittal is 'unsure'.

examples.pass: The submittal gives 50 x 20 x 5.75 in; the model's panel is 50 in high, 20 in wide and 5.75 in deep.
examples.fail: The submittal gives a 90 in high switchboard 36 in deep; the model's box is 90 x 40 x 20 in.

rules.check: Each device on a branch circuit is joined to its panel by that circuit's raceway or cable, end to end, and every drop ends on the device's box.
how: The prescreen (E-CONDUIT-CONTINUITY) followed each circuit's conduit sticks by their stored ends from the device's box to the panel's box: ends within `touch_in` meet, and a box their ends touch joins them. It never reads the router's report. Start from its findings.

A 'fail' names the gap: a drop that stops short of its box (by how many inches), a device no piece of its circuit reaches, or a raceway that never lands on its panel. Look at the device on the plan crop and in the model; a broken run is a 'fail' until it is rerouted.
A cable run (NM, MC) is followed by its pieces' links, because a cable's two ends aren't stored.

examples.pass: Receptacle on LP1-3: its drop ends on the box's top and the circuit's raceway runs unbroken to panel LP1.
examples.fail: The drop to the receptacle stops 12 in above its box; the receptacle isn't joined to its panel.

rules.check: Each raceway's conductors fill at most the share of its area NEC Chapter 9 Table 1 allows: 53% for one conductor, 31% for two, 40% for more.
how: The prescreen counted each raceway run's wires (count and size) against its trade size's area (Chapter 9 Tables 4 and 5, rules data). Start from its findings.
A raceway material or conductor size the tables don't list is 'unsure', never a pass.

examples.pass: Four #12 THHN and one #12 ground in 3/4" EMT: 0.067 sq in of 0.213 sq in allowed.
examples.fail: Four #4 THHN in 3/4" EMT: 0.33 sq in, 62% of the raceway.

rules.check: Each box holds what enters it (NEC 314.16(B)): each conductor entering counts once at its size's volume, all grounds once at the largest, a device yoke twice the largest conductor on it.
how: The prescreen counted the conductors of every raceway or cable whose end touches the box against the box's recorded volume. Start from its findings.
A box with no recorded volume, or a conductor size the table doesn't list, is 'unsure'.

examples.pass: A receptacle box of 22.5 cu in takes 4 #12, a ground and the yoke: 15.75 cu in.
examples.fail: A 4" square box of 21 cu in takes 8 #12, a ground and a yoke: 24.75 cu in.

rules.check: In each raceway with more than three current-carrying conductors, the NEC 310.15(C)(1) adjustment is applied: every conductor's adjusted ampacity (90 C column times the factor, never above the 75 C column, 110.14(C), nor the 240.4(D) limit) carries the largest breaker of the circuits in it.
how: The prescreen counted each raceway's current-carrying conductors (every one but the grounds), took the factor for that number from the rules data and the breakers from the panel schedule. Start from its findings.
A breaker the schedule doesn't give is 'unsure'. Feeder raceways are checked at their gear (E-GEAR-FILL).

examples.pass: Four #12 on 20 A breakers: 30 A x 0.8 = 24 A, limited to 20 A by 240.4(D): carries 20 A.
examples.fail: Four #8 on 50 A breakers: 55 A x 0.8 = 44 A, under 50 A.

rules.check: Each branch circuit's conductor size suits its length: the drawing's length table when it prints one (0-60' = #12), else at most 3% voltage drop (NEC 210.19(A) Informational Note 4) at the schedule's load.
how: The prescreen measured each circuit's length along its raceway from its panel to its farthest device (the sticks' own lengths) and took its smallest conductor. Start from its findings.
With no load in the schedule the rule's share of the breaker is used; a drop over 3% on that assumed load is 'unsure', not a fail.
A size the table doesn't cover, an unknown breaker or voltage is 'unsure'.

examples.pass: 130 ft on #8 at 16 A, 120 V: 1.0% drop.
examples.fail: The legend's table asks #10 from 60 to 100 ft; the circuit runs 85 ft on #12.

rules.check: Each run's wiring method (EMT, MC, NM…) is one the specification's wiring-methods table allows for the area it runs in (a guest or dwelling unit, an exposed room, concealed elsewhere), or the project's wiring-method rule, or an approved value-engineering alternative.
how: The prescreen took each run's method from its pieces' type and the area from the rooms its pieces are in, and the allowed methods from the specification's table as the job read it (26 05 19). Start from its findings.
No table read for an area is 'unsure', never a pass.

examples.pass: The guest-room branch is MC cable; the table allows MC concealed in units.
examples.fail: The corridor homerun is NM cable; the table allows EMT or MC concealed in common areas.

rules.check: No conduit comes within the clearance (rules data) of a duct, pipe, terminal, structure, equipment, other conduit, or a piece of gear's working space (NEC 110.26(A)); the router's own clash items are carried into the run.
how: The prescreen tested every conduit stick against the other trades' elements, the structure, the equipment and the gear's working space, each grown by its clearance, and against other runs' sticks away from where they meet. The router's clash items come in with source 'build'. Start from those findings.
Look at the spot on the plan and the section: a clash the build can't avoid needs a reroute or an RFI.

examples.pass: The homerun passes 3 in over a supply duct with 1 in clearance asked.
examples.fail: The tap runs through a 24 in return duct at 9.5 ft above the floor.

rules.check: The takeoff (the stored count index the BOM reads, and conduit.takeoff's lines) equals a recount of the model's pieces within takeoff_pct (1%): conduit feet by size from the sticks' ends, wire and cable feet, each fitting and box.
how: The prescreen recounted every raceway piece of the levels in scope and compared each kind, item and size with the stored index and conduit.takeoff. Start from its findings.
A line off by more than the tolerance is a 'fail': the index is stale (bim.count {refresh: true}) or the takeoff misses pieces.

examples.pass: 3/4" EMT: 412.6 ft recounted, 412.6 ft in the index and the takeoff.
examples.fail: EMT coupling 3/4": 14 recounted, 15 in the index.

rules.check: Luminaires are at their RCP positions, in the ceiling at that area's ceiling height (wall-mounted ones at the elevation or legend height), of the fixture schedule's type and mounted as the submittal says.
how: Compare each fixture on the RCP crop with the model picture: same place, same count.
Read the ceiling height for the area from the RCP tag; ceiling fixtures sit in that ceiling, wall fixtures at the elevation or legend height.
The type mark must be the fixture schedule row; the mounting (recessed, surface, pendant, wall) must match the schedule or submittal.

examples.pass: Four recessed fixtures in the RCP's grid are recessed in the 9 ft ceiling in the model.
examples.fail: A sconce shown on the elevation at mirror height is placed in the ceiling.

rules.check: Every luminaire's type tag has a row in the fixture schedule and a product in the lighting submittal, and its product fields (maker, catalog number, voltage, wattage, lumens, CCT, dimming, finish) are what they say; where the schedule and the submittal disagree it is a conflict citing both.
how: The prescreen gives each luminaire's type, its fixture schedule rows and its submittal product with each field's source, and its verdict: pass, fail (the model's product differs from the documents), conflict (the documents disagree: a plan tag with no schedule row, a scheduled type the submittal leaves out, a field the schedule and the cut sheet give differently) or unsure (no fixture schedule or submittal read).

Read the type tag beside the fixture on the RCP or lighting plan crop and find its row in the fixture schedule crop; compare the catalog number, voltage, lamp or lumens, CCT, dimming and mounting with the submittal's cut sheet page.
A conflict is the documents', not the model's: report the element 'unsure' and cite both documents, unless a print image settles which one holds.

examples.pass: Type A's schedule row and its cut sheet give the same catalog number, 0-10V driver and 3500K; the model's type A carries them.
examples.fail: The schedule and cut sheet give type B a 0-10V driver; the model's type B says non-dim.

rules.check: Every luminaire has a control (a switch, dimmer or sensor of its room on its switch leg, or one linked to it) unless it is marked emergency or unswitched.
how: The prescreen links each luminaire to the controls of its room by switch leg letter (or the link the model stores) and says which control, or why none is needed (an emergency, night light or unswitched marking, an exit sign).
On the lighting plan crop, find the switch leg letter beside the fixture and the switch with the same letter in the room; a fixture with no control and no emergency or unswitched marking is a 'fail'.

examples.pass: The two downlights on leg a are controlled by the dimmer on leg a by the door; the emergency fixture in the corridor needs no switch.
examples.fail: The bath light is on leg c, but no switch in the room is on leg c.

rules.check: Every switch, dimmer and occupancy or vacancy sensor controls luminaires of its own room or area by its switch leg.
how: The prescreen lists the luminaires each control reaches: the ones of its room with its switch leg letter (an unlettered control the unlettered ones), or the ones linked to it.
On the plan crop, the switch's subscript letter must match the letters at the fixtures it controls, in the same room; a leg with no fixture is a 'fail'.

examples.pass: Switch leg b by the bed controls the two sconces marked b in the same room.
examples.fail: The switch is on leg d but no fixture in the room is marked d.

rules.check: A dimmer controls only dimmable drivers of its own protocol (0-10 V, ELV, TRIAC, DALI); a dimmer on a non-dimmable driver or a protocol mismatch is a fail.
how: The prescreen reads each dimmer's protocol (its own type, the legend or the lighting controls schedule) and each controlled fixture's driver dimming (the model, the submittal's ordering row, the fixture schedule).

Check the lighting controls schedule and the fixture's cut sheet: a 0-10V driver needs a 0-10V dimmer with the control pair; an ELV or TRIAC dimmer can't dim it. 'Unsure' when either protocol is not stated.

examples.pass: The 0-10V dimmer controls two 0-10V downlights.
examples.fail: The dimmer controls a fixture whose cut sheet gives a non-dimming driver.

rules.check: Every 3-way switch has its mate (another 3-way switch on the same leg in its room); a 4-way switch stands between two 3-ways.
how: The prescreen finds 3-way and 4-way switches by their type words (the legend's '3-way' row, the type tag) and counts the set on each leg of each room.
On the plan crop, a 3-way switch at one door has its mate at the other door on the same leg; a lone 3-way is 'missing' its mate.

examples.pass: The 3-way switches at the entry and by the bed are both on leg a.
examples.fail: Only one 3-way switch is in the room; the plan shows a second at the bed.

rules.check: Per room, the model has as many luminaires and lighting controls of each type as the plan's symbols show.
how: The prescreen counts the plan's luminaire and control symbols in the room by type tag and the model's elements in it.
Where the counts differ, find the symbols on the RCP, lighting or enlarged plan crop: the model's missing ones are 'missing', the ones the plan doesn't show 'extra'.

examples.pass: The plan shows two type F sconces and a 3-way pair in the room; the model has the same.
examples.fail: The enlarged plan shows a type D fixture over the vanity; the model's room has none.

rules.check: Every fire alarm device the fire alarm plan or RCP shows in the area is in the model: detectors on the ceiling at their positions, notification appliances and pull stations in the wall at the legend height.
how: List each fire alarm symbol inside the area on the fire alarm plan or RCP crop; each must have a model element of a fire alarm kind near it (none is a 'missing' finding citing the crop).
Detectors: on the ceiling at the drawn place. Horns, strobes, speakers and pull stations: in the wall the symbol touches, at the mounting height of the fire alarm legend or general notes.
Compare positions, host and heights in the object list; a wall device on the ceiling, a detector on a wall, or a height outside the tolerance is a 'fail'.

examples.pass: The smoke detector is on the ceiling where the RCP shows it, and the horn strobe by the door is in the wall at the legend height.
examples.fail: The horn strobe is placed at receptacle height; the legend says high on the wall.

rules.check: The element's circuit and switch-leg tags are the print's.
how: Read the circuit number (panel and circuit) and switch leg letter beside each device or on its homerun on the plan crop.
Compare with the circuit and switch leg in the object list.
A different panel, circuit or leg is a 'fail'; no tag on the print and none in the model is a pass.

examples.pass: The plan tags the receptacle's homerun with circuit 12; the model's circuit is 12.
examples.fail: The plan tags switch leg a for the vanity light; the model has the vanity light on leg b.

rules.check: Every exhaust fan the plans show in the area is in the model, at the mechanical plan location in the room shown, in the ceiling (or at it), with the fan schedule's tag and airflow, and ducted to the discharge the print shows (shaft, exterior wall or roof).
how: Find each fan symbol and tag on the mechanical, enlarged or electrical plan (its equipment connection) inside the area; a fan with no model element is a 'missing' finding citing the crop. Confirm the room, and that the model fan is in the ceiling, not on the floor or a wall.
Look up the tag in the fan schedule (airflow, type) and compare with the object list.
Follow its duct on the plan to the discharge (shaft, wall cap, roof cap) and check the model's duct reaches the same discharge.

examples.pass: The bathroom fan is in the bathroom ceiling, schedule tag and airflow match, and its duct runs to the shaft as drawn.
examples.fail: The fan is in the closet next to the bathroom, or its duct ends in the ceiling space instead of the shaft.

rules.check: Duct follows the drawn route, connects the drawn terminals and equipment, and has no missing or extra segments.
how: Trace each duct on the mechanical plan crop from equipment to terminals.
Compare with the model overlay: the centerline stays within the route tolerance of the drawn duct.
Every drawn branch exists and ends at its terminal; a model segment with no drawn duct is 'extra'.

examples.pass: The supply main and its three branches follow the drawn route to the three diffusers.
examples.fail: One drawn branch is missing, leaving a diffuser unconnected.

rules.check: Each duct's size is the plan's size tag (width x height or diameter) and changes where the plan changes it.
how: Read the size tags along each duct on the plan crop and note where a size changes (transition symbol).
Compare with the sizes in the object list segment by segment.
A wrong size, or a size change in the wrong place, is a 'fail'.

examples.pass: The plan tags 12x8 then 10x6 after the first branch; the model changes at the same branch.
examples.fail: The model runs the whole main at 12x8.

rules.check: Duct runs in the ceiling space (above the ceiling, below the structure) or at the height a section or note gives.
how: Read the ceiling height of the area from the RCP and any duct elevation from sections or notes.
In the model's elevation or 3D view, the duct must be above the ceiling and below the structure.
A duct through the ceiling, under it, or through the structure is a 'fail'.

examples.pass: The duct bottom is above the ceiling and its top below the joists.
examples.fail: The duct hangs below the corridor's lowered ceiling.

rules.check: Diffusers and grilles are at their RCP or mechanical plan positions, of the schedule's type and airflow.
how: Compare each terminal on the RCP or mechanical plan with the model: same place, same count.
Read the tag and airflow beside the symbol and the matching schedule row.
Compare type and airflow in the object list.

examples.pass: Two supply diffusers at the RCP positions, schedule type and airflow match.
examples.fail: A return grille is modelled as a supply diffuser.

rules.check: Equipment is at the drawn location, of the schedule or submittal size, with its service clearance kept clear.
how: Find the equipment symbol and tag on the plan crop; compare its place with the model.
Read the size from the schedule or submittal page and compare the model's size.
Check that nothing in the model stands in the service clearance the submittal shows.
A fan coil unit is equipment (this rule), not an exhaust fan: check it where the mechanical plan draws it (ceiling, closet or soffit), with its schedule tag and size, and its access panel clear.

examples.pass: The unit is in the closet where drawn, the size matches the submittal, and the access side is clear.
examples.fail: A wall in the model blocks the unit's filter access side.

rules.check: Plumbing fixtures are where the architectural and plumbing plans show them, of the fixture schedule's type.
how: Compare each fixture on the enlarged architectural plan and the plumbing plan with the model.
Read each fixture's tag and its fixture schedule row.
Compare type and place in the object list.

examples.pass: The lavatory and water closet are where the enlarged plan draws them, schedule types match.
examples.fail: The tub is modelled where the plan shows a shower.

rules.check: Water, waste and vent piping is present for every fixture's room as the plumbing plans and risers show, at the tagged sizes.
how: For each fixture in the area, find its water, waste and vent lines on the plumbing plan and riser diagram.
Check each line exists in the model and reaches the fixture or its riser.
Compare sizes with the size tags.

examples.pass: The lavatory has hot, cold, waste and vent lines to the riser at the tagged sizes.
examples.fail: The vent line drawn on the riser is missing from the model.

rules.check: Every PTAC or through-wall unit the plans show in the area is in the model, in an exterior wall (its sleeve through that wall, usually under the window), of the schedule's tag.
how: Find each PTAC or through-wall unit symbol and tag on the mechanical or enlarged plan inside the area; one with no model element is a 'missing' finding citing the crop.
The object list gives the unit's host wall: it must be a wall of the building's outside face (the plan's exterior wall, the side with the windows), not an interior partition.
Read its tag and schedule row (capacity, sleeve size) and compare with the object list; a unit on an interior wall or away from any wall is a 'fail'.

examples.pass: The guest room's unit sits in the exterior wall under the window where the enlarged plan draws it, tagged as the schedule row.
examples.fail: The unit is modelled on the corridor wall; the plan draws it in the exterior wall.

rules.check: Every thermostat the plans show in the area is in the model, on the wall the plan draws it on (at its wall face), at the height the legend, elevation or notes give, for the unit the plans pair it with.
how: Find each thermostat symbol (T, TSTAT) on the mechanical, enlarged or electrical plan inside the area; one with no model element is a 'missing' finding citing the crop, and a model thermostat no symbol stands for is 'extra'.
The object list gives its host wall and its distance to the wall face (G-HOST in `prescreen`): it must be on the wall the plan draws it on, not in the room's middle or on the far side of the wall.
Compare its height above the floor with the legend, elevation or general notes (G-HEIGHT in `prescreen` names the document); a default height no document gives is 'unsure', never a pass.
Check it controls the unit the plans pair it with (its tag, or the unit in the same room).

examples.pass: The thermostat is on the wall by the entry where the enlarged plan draws it, at its wall face, at the legend's 48 in. to its centre.
examples.fail: The thermostat stands in the middle of the room, 4 ft from any wall, or sits at the 18 in. receptacle height.

rules.check: Every occupancy or vacancy sensor the plans show in the area is in the model, hosted as the legend says: in the wall at switch height for a wall sensor, on the ceiling for a ceiling sensor.
how: List each occupancy or vacancy sensor symbol inside the area on the lighting plan, enlarged plan or RCP crop; one with no model element is a 'missing' finding citing the crop.
Read the legend row of its symbol: wall-mounted (a switch-box sensor) or ceiling-mounted.
In the object list a wall sensor is in the wall the symbol touches at the legend or switch height, a ceiling sensor on the ceiling; the other way round is a 'fail'.

examples.pass: The vacancy sensor by the bathroom door is in the wall at switch height, as the legend's wall sensor row says.
examples.fail: The ceiling occupancy sensor of the meeting room is modelled as a wall device by the door.

rules.check: Every equipment connection the electrical plans show in the area is in the model at the equipment it serves, of the equipment its tag names.
how: Find each equipment connection symbol (the connection to a fan, unit, heater or other equipment) and its tag inside the area on the power or enlarged plan; one with no model element is a 'missing' finding citing the crop.
Read what its tag is from the equipment schedule or legend; the model's connection must sit at that equipment (an exhaust fan's in the ceiling, a through-wall unit's at the exterior wall).
A connection away from its equipment, or tagged as other equipment than the plan says, is a 'fail'.

examples.pass: The bathroom exhaust fan's connection is in the bathroom ceiling, tagged as the fan in the schedule.
examples.fail: The connection tagged for the bathroom fan is modelled in the closet next to it.

rules.check: Sprinkler heads are at their RCP or fire protection plan positions when the prints draw them.
how: If the RCP or fire protection plan draws heads in the area, compare each with the model.
If heads are not drawn (design by others), say so and mark the rule 'unsure' rather than guess.
Compare count and place.

examples.pass: Two heads on the RCP, two heads in the model at the same places.
examples.fail: The RCP draws a head over the closet; the model has none there.
